blocks.text: Haemophilia is a rare X-linked recessive disorder in which the blood fails to clot properly after an injury, because blood clotting factors are reduced, malfunctioning or absent. It is of three types.

blocks.caption: Types of haemophilia
rows: X-linked recessive; more common in males
X-linked recessive; more common in males
Autosomal recessive; equal in both sexes

items: When an injury occurs, platelets stick to the site and form a platelet plug.
Activated platelets and the damaged tissue release clotting factors.
The clotting factors carry out a chain of reactions (the clotting cascade) in which the soluble protein fibrinogen is converted into insoluble fibrin.
Fibrin forms a mesh that traps parts of the blood and makes a solid clot.
The clot is stabilized by cross-linking of the fibrin strands.

blocks.text: If the balance of the clotting system is disturbed, abnormal clotting called thrombosis can occur, which can cause serious problems such as stroke and heart attack.

People with normal (trichromatic) vision have three kinds of cone cell in the retina, each sensitive to one primary colour: red-sensitive, green-sensitive and blue-sensitive cones, each with its own pigment proteins called opsins. The genes for the red and green opsins are on the X chromosome and the gene for the blue opsin on autosome 7; recessive alleles of these opsin genes cause colour-blindness.

blocks.alt: Top: normal trichromatic vision with red, green and blue cones; boxes say the red and green opsin genes are on the X chromosome and the blue opsin gene on chromosome 7. Middle: dichromacy, three sets of cones each with one missing: protanopia (no red), deuteranopia (no green) and tritanopia (no blue). Bottom: monochromacy, two opsins missing; blue-cone monochromacy lacks red and green opsins.
blocks.caption: Cone opsins, dichromacy and monochromacy (original diagram after Figure 18.18).
blocks.long_description: Normal (trichromatic) vision uses three kinds of cone cell in the retina, sensitive to red, green and blue light, each with its own opsin pigment protein. The red and green opsin genes are on the X chromosome and the blue opsin gene on chromosome 7; recessive alleles of these genes cause colour-blindness. In dichromacy one opsin is missing, so the person sees two primary colours and is blind to the third: protanopia (red), deuteranopia (green) or tritanopia (blue). In monochromacy two opsins are missing; in blue-cone monochromacy the red and green opsins are absent, while red-cone and green-cone monochromacy are very rare.

items: Dichromacy: perception of two primary colours and blindness to the third, whose opsin is missing: red-blindness (protanopia), green-blindness (deuteranopia) or blue-blindness (tritanopia).

Monochromacy (total colour-blindness): perception of a single colour and blindness to the two whose opsins are missing. In blue-cone monochromacy the red and green opsins are absent; red-cone and green-cone monochromacy are very rare.

blocks.title: Red-green colour-blindness
blocks.text: Blue-cone monochromacy, in which the red and green opsins are absent, is also called red-green colour-blindness.

There is no cure for colour-blindness, but assistive technologies such as colour-blind glasses and special software help people tell colours apart, and some have succeeded with colour-discrimination training.

More than 30 disorders are classified as muscular dystrophies, and Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most common. It is X-linked recessive, so it is more common in males; about two thirds of cases are inherited from the mother and one third come from a new mutation. A male who receives the recessive allele cannot make the muscle protein dystrophin, so muscle fibres die and the skeletal muscles weaken and break down, first those of the hips, pelvic area, thighs and calves, later the shoulders and neck, arms, respiratory and cardiac muscles and other areas.

blocks.alt: Three body outlines with affected muscles shaded purple: first the hips, pelvis, thighs and calves; later also the shoulders and arms; late also the chest, for breathing and heart muscle. A timeline gives about age 4 weakness as the child walks, by 10 braces, by 12 a wheelchair, and a typical lifespan of 15 to 45. A box gives the cause and treatments.
blocks.caption: The course of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (original diagram after Figure 18.19).
blocks.long_description: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the most common of more than 30 muscular dystrophies, is X-linked recessive, so it is far more common in boys; about two thirds of cases are inherited from the mother and one third come from a new mutation. An affected boy cannot make the muscle protein dystrophin, so muscle fibres die. Weakness begins in the hips, pelvis, thighs and calves at about age four, when walking starts, then spreads to the shoulders, neck, arms, and the breathing and heart muscles. Braces may be needed by 10 and most boys use a wheelchair by 12; typical lifespans are 15 to 45 years. There is no cure; physiotherapy, corticosteroids, pain relief and surgery for joint contractures help manage it.

blocks.text: It affects a child around the age of four and becomes evident when the child begins walking. By age 10 the child may need braces, and by 12 most patients cannot walk and need a wheelchair. Typical lifespans range from 15 to 45 years. There is no cure, but treatment manages the symptoms: physical therapy maintains strength, flexibility and mobility; corticosteroids give short-term improvement in muscle strength; pain-killers relieve muscle pain; and surgery corrects joint contractures.
Embryonic screening means methods that check embryos for genetic disorders and an abnormal number of chromosomes, such as ultrasound scanning, chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis.

Amniocentesis is generally done between the 15th and 20th weeks of pregnancy. A long needle is inserted into the amniotic sac while an ultrasound probe locates the foetus; the needle draws out some amniotic fluid containing foetal cells, which are kept in a culture medium and checked for an abnormal number of chromosomes.
